scope_note: 3.1 is INTERPRETING the table (code, prefix, mask, next hop, AD, metric, gateway of last resort). Items that require simulating a packet's path belong to 3.2, not here.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. According to the output, what administrative distance is associated with R1's route to 192.168.20.0/24?

exhibit.content:
R1# show ip route
Codes: L - local, C - connected, S - static, R - RIP, M - mobile, B - BGP
       D - EIGRP, EX - EIGRP external, O - OSPF, IA - OSPF inter area
       N1 - OSPF NSSA external type 1, N2 - OSPF NSSA external type 2
       E1 - OSPF external type 1, E2 - OSPF external type 2
       i - IS-IS, su - IS-IS summary, L1 - IS-IS level-1, L2 - IS-IS level-2
       ia - IS-IS inter area, * - candidate default, U - per-user static route
       o - ODR, P - periodic downloaded static route, H - NHRP, l - LISP
       a - application route
       + - replicated route, % - next hop override

Gateway of last resort is not set

      10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 4 subnets, 2 masks
C        10.1.1.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
L        10.1.1.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
C        10.1.2.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
L        10.1.2.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
D     192.168.10.0/24 [90/2172416] via 10.1.1.2, 00:04:11, GigabitEthernet0/0
O     192.168.20.0/24 [110/65] via 10.1.2.2, 00:09:53, GigabitEthernet0/1

items.explanation: In show ip route the bracketed pair is always [administrative distance/metric], so the OSPF entry [110/65] carries an administrative distance of 110. Option A takes 65, which is the OSPF cost, and reverses the two bracket fields. Option B quotes 2172416, the composite metric belonging to the EIGRP row for 192.168.10.0/24, so it reads the correct field from the wrong row. Option D quotes 90, the administrative distance shown on that same EIGRP row, another wrong-row read.

options.text: 110 is the administrative distance of the entry; the OSPF cost shown for it is 74.
110 is the OSPF cost of the entry; the administrative distance shown for it is 74.
110 is the hop count that OSPF inherited from the RIP entry above it in the table.
110 is a composite metric, because OSPF entries are not assigned an administrative distance.

items.explanation: The bracket prints [administrative distance/metric]. For 192.168.40.0/24 that is [110/74], so 110 is the administrative distance and 74 is the OSPF cost. Option B simply reverses the two fields, the single commonest misreading of this output. Option C imports the hop-count metric idea from the RIP entry [120/3] above and applies it to OSPF, confusing one protocol's metric type with another's. Option D asserts that OSPF has no administrative distance, when every installed entry is selected using one.

items.explanation: The legend defines * as candidate default, and the header line confirms the result: gateway of last resort is 203.0.113.1 to network 0.0.0.0. Option A confuses the asterisk with a floating or inactive static, but an unusable route is not installed in the table at all. Option B misreads the S code, which denotes a statically configured route, not a dynamically learned one. Option C invents redistribution, which the output never indicates and which the asterisk does not signify.

items.explanation: The banner is a header for the child entries: six subnets of 10.0.0.0/8 are present and they use three distinct masks, which the output bears out with /30, /24 and /32 prefixes. Option A misreads "3 masks" as duplicate routes and contradicts "variably", which means the subnets are deliberately unequal in size. Option C confuses this header with route summarisation, an advertisement behaviour the routing table does not describe. Option D invents classful behaviour; a classful protocol could not produce three different masks here at all.

Option B confuses the local route with an ARP-derived host entry for a neighbouring device, but the table shows the router's own address. Option C reads L as loopback, an extremely common misreading of the code letter. Option D borrows IPv6 link-local addressing and applies it to an IPv4 table where no such entry exists.

L        10.1.1.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
O     209.165.201.0/24 [110/2] via 10.1.1.2, 00:15:41, GigabitEthernet0/0
O IA  192.168.5.0/24 [110/66] via 10.1.1.2, 00:15:41, GigabitEthernet0/0

items.explanation: The code O E2 means OSPF external type 2, which is how a prefix redistributed into OSPF from an outside source appears, so 198.51.100.0/24 is the answer. Option A is coded plain O, an intra-area route learned inside the router's own area. Option B is coded O IA, an inter-area route that crossed from another OSPF area but is still inside the OSPF domain, which is the distinction this item targets. Option D is coded C, a directly connected subnet that OSPF never learned at all.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. The static route to 192.168.50.0/24 specifies a next-hop address but no exit interface. Which entry in the table must R7 resolve in order to determine an outgoing interface for that static route?

exhibit.content:
R7# show ip route
Codes: L - local, C - connected, S - static, R - RIP, M - mobile, B - BGP
       D - EIGRP, EX - EIGRP external, O - OSPF, IA - OSPF inter area
       N1 - OSPF NSSA external type 1, N2 - OSPF NSSA external type 2
       E1 - OSPF external type 1, E2 - OSPF external type 2
       i - IS-IS, su - IS-IS summary, L1 - IS-IS level-1, L2 - IS-IS level-2
       ia - IS-IS inter area, * - candidate default, U - per-user static route
       o - ODR, P - periodic downloaded static route, H - NHRP, l - LISP
       a - application route
       + - replicated route, % - next hop override

Gateway of last resort is not set

      10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 3 subnets, 2 masks
C        10.1.1.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
L        10.1.1.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
O        10.1.1.4/30 [110/128] via 10.1.1.2, 00:22:07, GigabitEthernet0/0
S     192.168.50.0/24 [1/0] via 10.1.1.6

options.text: 10.1.1.0/30, because a static next hop must sit on a directly connected subnet.
10.1.1.4/30, because that entry's range covers the next hop 10.1.1.6.
10.1.1.1/32, because the local route identifies the router's own outgoing interface.
No entry, because the static route is already directly attached via GigabitEthernet0/0.

items.explanation: A next-hop-only static route is recursive: R7 looks up the next hop 10.1.1.6, which falls inside 10.1.1.4/30 (hosts .5 and .6), and inherits that entry's outgoing interface. Option A asserts the next hop must be directly connected, a widespread misconception that recursion exists precisely to relax. Option C picks the L /32 for the router's own address, which describes R7 itself and can never resolve a remote next hop. Option D denies recursion entirely and misreads the static as a connected route.

options.text: R8 installed the first path only and holds the second in reserve until the primary fails.
The repeated entry shows an OSPF adjacency flapping between the two neighbours.

R8 installed both paths and will share traffic for that prefix across them.

items.explanation: Both paths show [110/74], so their cost is equal and OSPF installs both as equal-cost paths that share the load. Option A describes a floating route held out of the table, but a backup path with a worse distance would not be printed here at all. Option B reads duplication as instability, yet both paths show a matching 00:31:16 uptime, which indicates stability rather than flapping. Option C invents a numerically-lowest-next-hop tie-break, borrowing a bridge-ID style comparison that OSPF does not apply to installed routes.

Option B at /13 is the broadest entry in the whole table, and picking it treats a smaller number as more specific, inverting the comparison. Option C at /24 is the closest rival and is the answer only if the /26 line is overlooked.

options.text: The three destinations sit at different hop counts, which the values count.

A larger value means the destination lies further from R12 in router hops.

items.explanation: The second bracket field is the metric of whichever protocol installed the entry, and the three protocols measure entirely different things: RIP counts hops, EIGRP composes bandwidth and delay, OSPF sums interface cost. Comparing 3 against 2172416 is therefore meaningless. Options A and C both read every value as a hop count, which holds only for the RIP entry. Option D confuses the two bracket fields, since the administrative distances are the first values, 120, 90 and 110.

items.explanation: The code combines three facts: O means OSPF learned it, E2 means it is an external type 2 route injected from outside the OSPF domain, and the asterisk marks it as the candidate default. Option A would require the code S, since a locally configured default appears as a static route. Option B ignores the E2, which is precisely what rules out an intra-area origin. Option C describes an inter-area route, which would carry the code IA rather than E2.
